Palaemon elegans from intertidal pools along the European Atlantic coast display a maximum recorded total body length of 5.84 centimeters [Li = 5.84 centimeters], a size that appears to represent an upper limit for this species across much of its range. Females attain sexual maturity at a significantly smaller body size, with the smallest total length of shrimp with eggs recorded at 3.65 cm [Lp = 3.65 cm], marking the onset of reproductive capability. This substantial disparity between puberty length and ultimate length suggests that individuals invest heavily in somatic growth even after initiating reproduction, a pattern common among caridean shrimp facing variable resource availability in ephemeral rock pool habitats. Morphometric surveys conducted along the Portuguese coast confirm that both sexes can achieve the maximal dimensions, although females typically predominate in the larger size classes. The relationship between body length and dry mass is well described by a power function, with ultimate dry weight reaching 0.398 grams  in the largest specimens, reflecting the relatively slender body plan of this palaemonid shrimp when compared to more robust congeneric species occupying subtidal environments.

Newly hatched larvae emerge at a remarkably small size, with wet weight at birth calculated from egg dimensions as 0.000085 grams [Wwb = 0.000085 grams], a value derived from the spherical volume formula using an egg length of 0.65 millimeters and an egg width of 0.5 millimeters. This minuscule neonatal mass, equivalent to roughly 0.085 milligrams, places Rockpool shrimp among the lighter-bodied caridean larvae and imposes tight constraints on the initial feeding ecology of the newly released planktonic stages. In stark contrast, the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults reaches 1.43 grams [Wwi = 1.43 grams], representing a more than sixteen-thousand-fold increase from birth to maximal body size. The wet weight at puberty is 0.500 grams [Wwp = 0.500 grams], which corresponds closely to the smallest gravid females captured in breeding condition; this threshold mass appears to be a robust indicator of the onset of ovarian maturation across distinct populations. A comparative analysis of weight data from the Bay of Biscay indicates that the relationship between wet and dry mass remains relatively constant throughout juvenile development, with water content averaging close to seventy-two percent of the total body weight.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], females achieve a maximum reproductive rate of 1704 eggs per year [Ri = 1704 eggs per year], a fecundity figure that translates to roughly 4.67 eggs per day when averaged across the annual cycle. This elevated reproductive output is facilitated by the rapid maturation of successive clutches of brood eggs within the ovigerous female, allowing continuous breeding throughout the warm summer months when phytoplankton blooms sustain the filter-feeding nauplius larvae. This same temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] also governs the developmental pace of the yolk-dependent embryo, with the time since birth at metamorphosis recorded as 22 days since birth  under these thermal conditions. This relatively short larval duration, spanning the period from hatching through the morphological transformation of the free-swimming zoea larva to the benthic decapodid stage, is characteristic of species exploiting ephemeral intertidal pools where rapid recruitment is essential for population persistence. Metabolic rates at this temperature are elevated, accelerating both the depletion of endogenous yolk reserves and the onset of first exogenous feeding in the actively growing larva.

At a cooler but seasonally relevant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], developmental processes slow considerably: the age at birth, defined as the interval from egg fertilisation through hatching of the planktonic larva, extends to approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], reflecting the reduced metabolic rates typical of palaemonid embryogenesis at sub-optimal thermal regimes. The maximum lifespan recorded under these conditions reaches 400 days [am = 400 days], a longevity estimate originally derived from comparative data on the closely related grass shrimp Palaemonetes pugio and subsequently validated by mark-recapture studies in southern English rock pools at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This life span of roughly 13 months positions Rockpool shrimp as a relatively short-lived caridean, with high annual turnover driven by intense predation pressure from fish and shorebirds as well as the physiological demands of repeated spawning events. Field observations suggest that senescence in this species is characterized by a progressive decline in molting frequency and a reduced capacity for limb regeneration, ultimately leading to natural mortality during winter storms or periods of extreme desiccation. The 20 °C [T = 20 °C] thermal regime also influences the post-larval juvenile stage, with growth rates diminishing markedly as individuals approach the asymptotic body mass.

The interplay between temperature-dependent development and reproductive scheduling is strikingly illustrated by the metamorphic transition: under 26 °C [T = 26 °C] conditions, the larval-juvenile transformation is completed within a 22-day interval following hatching (22 days following hatching) , a period during which the planktonic megalopa larva undergoes dramatic allometric shifts in body plan reorganising the appendages for benthic life. This abbreviated larval phase confers a distinct advantage in the highly variable intertidal zone, enabling juvenile recruitment before seasonal desiccation events or thermal extremes can decimate the free-swimming cohort. A parallel can be drawn with the reproductive timing of adult females: the combination of achieving sexual maturation at a body length of 3.65 cm [Lp = 3.65 cm] and attaining a body mass of 0.500 grams [Wwp = 0.500 grams] ensures that only individuals with sufficient energetic reserves can sustain the production of viable brood eggs. Ultimately, the species' life-history strategy, characterised by a maximum size of 5.84 centimeters [Li = 5.84 centimeters] and a maximum lifespan of 400 days [am = 400 days] under 20 °C [T = 20 °C], reflects an adaptation to unpredictable habitats where early reproduction at a relatively modest body size outweighs the benefits of prolonged somatic growth.
